payload.rationale: No current data were supplied, so this is a prior-based judgment. Observed background: through late 2025 the Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year average had drifted down to roughly the low-to-mid 6% range after Fed easing, and most institutional forecasts for 2026 centered on roughly 6.0–6.6%. Weekly PMMS moves are small (typically under 10–15 bp), so the Sep 24, 2026 print will be very close to the level prevailing in mid-September 2026, which I cannot observe. For the rate to exceed 7.01%, rates would need to have risen materially (roughly 50–100 bp) from late-2025 levels, which would require a meaningful inflation/term-premium shock or a hawkish Fed repricing. That is plausible but not the base case. The existence of a 7.01% strike suggests it is within the offered range, but such ranges usually include tail strikes. Too-high risk: if rates in 2026 actually stayed near or below 6.5%, a 7.01%+ print is nearly impossible in a single week, and the true probability would be near zero. Too-low risk: if a 2026 bond selloff (fiscal concerns, sticky inflation, tariff-driven price pressures) had already pushed mortgage rates to the high-6s or above 7% by September 2026, the probability could be well above 50%, since week-to-week persistence is very high. Overall I assign a low probability reflecting the base-case outlook while leaving room for an unobserved upward regime shift.
limitations: No current research or recent PMMS values supplied; forecast relies on background knowledge that ends well before September 2026.
Cannot observe Treasury yields, Fed policy path, or mortgage spreads as of mid-September 2026.
Strike placement may hint at the prevailing level but is not evidence of likelihood.
Weekly PMMS value is highly persistent, so error is dominated by uncertainty about the unobserved current level rather than weekly noise.
